cases.title: Employee, university and public-disclosure facts
cases.prompt:
We are developing an Ayurvedic wound-care gel in India. Our employee created the extraction process during paid work, a university laboratory optimized stability under a collaboration agreement, and a freelance designer made our label. At a trade fair six months ago we publicly showed the gel and handed out a leaflet naming the ingredients, but we did not disclose extraction temperatures or ratios. We now want to patent the process, keep remaining know-how confidential, register the name and protect the packaging.

Before proposing a strategy, identify the facts that could change ownership or patentability and explain why each matters. Distinguish inventorship from ownership, patentability from freedom to operate, prior public disclosure from remaining secrecy, and artwork copyright from functional packaging design. Do not assume the company owns the university work. Give conditional outcomes and exact Indian statutory citations. Explicitly mark any point the corpus cannot support.

YOUR QUESTION
 We are developing an Ayurvedic wound-care gel in India. Our employee created the extraction process during paid work, a university laboratory optimized stability under a collaboration agreement, and a freelance designer made our label. At a trade fair six months ago we publicly showed the gel and handed out a leaflet naming the ingredients, but we did not disclose extraction temperatures or ratios. We now want to patent the process, keep remaining know-how confidential, register the name and protect the packaging.

Before proposing a strategy, identify the facts that could change ownership or patentability and explain why each matters. Distinguish inventorship from ownership, patentability from freedom to operate, prior public disclosure from remaining secrecy, and artwork copyright from functional packaging design. Do not assume the company owns the university work. Give conditional outcomes and exact Indian statutory citations. Explicitly mark any point the corpus cannot support.

India
18 cited sources
Reviewed local guidance
Records: 1957-01-21 – 2026-09-27

Facts supplied by you (unverified)

“We are developing an Ayurvedic wound-care gel in India.”
“Our employee created the extraction process during paid work, a university laboratory optimized stability under a collaboration agreement, and a freelance designer made our label.”
“At a trade fair six months ago we publicly showed the gel and handed out a leaflet naming the ingredients, but we did not disclose extraction temperatures or ratios.”
“We now want to patent the process, keep remaining know-how confidential, register the name and protect the packaging.”

Facts still needed and conditional outcomes

What precise formulation or process features would be claimed, and what prior-art comparison and experimental data support the claimed technical contribution? Inference/application: An independently developed product/process still needs a claim-specific novelty, inventive-step and industrial-applicability assessment (ss.2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 2(1)(l)) 13 Compare the proposed claims with traditional knowledge and the known properties of traditionally known components; a new product description does not establish that this exclusion is overcome. (s.3(p)) 15 A mixture that only adds the known effects of its herbs may fail this exclusion; evidence of an interaction beyond that aggregation is relevant to the assessment. (s.3(e)) 16 Review this exclusion if the proposed claim concerns a new form, use or process involving a known substance; a new label or dosage is not enough to decide patentability. (s.3(d)) 17
What information has been disclosed, to whom, on what dates and under what confidentiality terms, and has any patent application already been filed? Inference/application: You report a public disclosure: “At a trade fair six months ago we publicly showed the gel and handed out a leaflet naming the ingredients” Assess precisely what that display, publication or handout made available, its date and any specific statutory exception. A general grace period cannot be assumed. You separately state “we did not disclose extraction temperatures or ratios.” Distinguish those undisclosed details from the disclosed product and ingredients; do not assume that showing the product disclosed every process parameter or that keeping some details private cures the earlier disclosure. (ss.2(1)(l), 9(1), 11A, 29-34) 8 A patent strategy requires sufficient disclosure and the relevant best method; secrecy cannot substitute for information needed to support the claimed invention (s.10(4)(a)-(c); s.10(4)(d) proviso (ii)(D); ss.25(1)(j), 64(1)(p)) 5 For the covered proprietary medicine, mandatory ingredient-label disclosures limit what formulation information can remain secret on sale; assess undisclosed process know-how separately (s.33EEC(a)(ii); r.161(1)) 3
What exact features did the stated contributors create, and what do their employment, collaboration, funding and assignment documents say? Inference/application: You report “Our employee created the extraction process during paid work, a university laboratory optimized stability under a collaboration agreement, and a freelance designer made our label.” Identify the human contributors to the claimed invention separately from the person or entity entitled to apply. If the company relies on assignment of the right to apply, it needs the applicable proof while the inventor remains identified. Employment, payment and a university collaboration do not supply that proof in this record. The company's claimed title remains unresolved until the contributions and chain of title are checked; mention as inventor does not itself confer patent rights. (ss.6, 7(2)-(3), 10(6), 28(1)) 6 For a transaction in an existing patent, assess the written, duly executed instrument and registration of the acquired title or interest under these provisions. Keep that separate from proof of an assignment of the right to apply before grant. Inspect the actual employment, university and other agreements for invention scope, retained rights and execution; payment or a confidentiality clause does not establish the required assignment here. These patent provisions do not decide copyright ownership of artwork. (ss.68, 69(1)-(3)) 11

Patent eligibility for the formulation and process

Established by source: A patentable invention must be a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application; the Act separately defines inventive step and new invention. (India; ss.2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 2(1)(l)) 13 Section 48 provides the specified exclusive rights for patented products and processes in India; ss.73–74 identify the Controller of Patents and Patent Office. (India; ss.48, 73-74) 4

Inference/application: Assess the specific formulation or manufacturing-process claims for novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability. The stated development history or a new product label does not establish those tests. 13 A patent may protect qualifying product/process claims, but does not itself establish regulatory permission to sell or freedom to operate against other patents. 4

Not established by retrieved sources: No prior-art search, claim analysis or experimental evidence has established that this particular invention satisfies those tests. The scope of proposed claims, third-party rights and regulatory clearance require separate assessments.

Patent exclusions

Established by source: Traditional knowledge, and aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components, are excluded from inventions by s.3(p). (India; s.3(p)) 15 Section 3(e) excludes a mere admixture giving only an aggregation of component properties and a process for producing that substance. (India; s.3(e)) 16 Section 3(d) excludes a new form of a known substance without enhancement of known efficacy and other specified discoveries involving known substances or processes. (India; s.3(d)) 17 Section 3(c) excludes the mere discovery of a scientific principle or abstract theory, or discovery of any living thing or non-living substance occurring in nature. (India; s.3(c)) 18 Section 3(i) excludes processes for specified medicinal and other treatment of humans and similar treatment of animals. (India; s.3(i)) 12 Section 3(j) excludes plants and animals in whole or part, including seeds, varieties and species, and essentially biological production or propagation processes, subject to its micro-organism exception. (India; s.3(j)) 14

Inference/application: Compare the proposed claims with traditional knowledge and the known properties of traditionally known components; a new product description does not establish that this exclusion is overcome. 15 A mixture that only adds the known effects of its herbs may fail this exclusion; evidence of an interaction beyond that aggregation is relevant to the assessment. 16 Review this exclusion if the proposed claim concerns a new form, use or process involving a known substance; a new label or dosage is not enough to decide patentability. 17 Merely discovering a naturally occurring plant substance does not establish an invention; a claimed technical product or process must be assessed independently. 18 A claim to a treatment or administration regimen can engage this exclusion; a product or manufacturing-process claim must be assessed on its own terms. 12 A plant, plant part or variety is not made patentable simply by being used in a new medicine; formulation/process eligibility requires a separate assessment. 14

Not established by retrieved sources: Whether the proposed claims merely reproduce traditional knowledge requires a claim-specific prior-art comparison. The sources do not establish that this formulation has such an effect or that evidence of synergy alone would guarantee a patent. The identity of the known substance, the precise claims and the relevant efficacy evidence are not supplied. Whether the claim is only to a natural discovery or to a qualifying technical invention depends on the actual claim and supporting evidence. No proposed claim wording is available to determine whether a dosage feature is claimed as a product feature or a treatment method. The exact subject matter of any plant-related claims remains unspecified.

Trade secrets and confidentiality before filing

Established by source: Confidential know-how may be protected through trade-secret/confidentiality arrangements; this is distinct from registration of a patent. (India; Sections 1-3 and 5 of the WIPO India country overview; Contract Act s.73 and Specific Relief Act s.38 discussed) 1 A complete specification must sufficiently describe the invention, its operation/use and performance method, disclose the best method known to the applicant, and define the claims. Section 10(4) also addresses source and geographical origin of biological material used in the invention. (India; s.10(4)(a)-(c); s.10(4)(d) proviso (ii)(D); ss.25(1)(j), 64(1)(p)) 5 Section 11A provides for publication of patent applications subject to its exceptions; the Act's anticipation provisions contain specific, limited exceptions for certain disclosures. (India; ss.2(1)(l), 9(1), 11A, 29-34) 8 The ASU provisions require a true ingredient list; Rule 161 requires patent/proprietary ASU labels to disclose the specified ingredient particulars, including botanical names, parts, form and quantity, with a separate enclosed list permitted in the prescribed circumstances. (India; s.33EEC(a)(ii); r.161(1)) 3

Inference/application: A process that can remain confidential may be suitable for secrecy; readily discoverable product composition and information that a patent must disclose need a different assessment. 1 Trade secrecy cannot replace disclosures required to support the invention claimed in a patent; biological-material provenance must be considered in drafting. 5 You report a public disclosure: “At a trade fair six months ago we publicly showed the gel and handed out a leaflet naming the ingredients” Assess precisely what that display, publication or handout made available, its date and any specific statutory exception. A general grace period cannot be assumed. You separately state “we did not disclose extraction temperatures or ratios.” Distinguish those undisclosed details from the disclosed product and ingredients; do not assume that showing the product disclosed every process parameter or that keeping some details private cures the earlier disclosure. 8 A proprietary formulation cannot simply be kept wholly secret after compliant sale where ingredient quantities must be disclosed. Assess confidential process know-how separately. 3

Not established by retrieved sources: Whether secrecy is commercially effective, whether information is actually confidential, and the enforceability of specific agreements require professional review. Which process details are necessary for sufficient disclosure, and any applicable deposit requirements, require review of the actual invention. The supplied disclosure/secrecy account needs documentary verification: the actual display or publication and handout, precise dates, recipients, confidentiality terms, filing history and any applicable statutory exception. Its effect on each proposed claim has not been established. The actual label, formulation and applicable labelling particulars need regulatory review.

Trademark protection and its limits

Established by source: Trade marks distinguish the commercial origin of goods or services. Distinctiveness and the refusal grounds in s.9 matter; a descriptive or generic product name may not qualify. (India; ss.2(1)(zb),3-5,9,11,18,25,28) 9

Inference/application: A distinctive product brand, logo or qualifying get-up can be considered for protection; trademark rights do not protect the medicinal formula, extraction technique or manufacturing method. 9

Not established by retrieved sources: Availability of the proposed mark, competing marks and the correct goods/services specification have not been checked.

Copyright

Established by source: Copyright subsists in the original works specified by s.13, including literary and artistic works; ownership and registration are separate questions under the Act. (India; ss.13,14,17-19,44-45,48) 2 The Government Copyright Office handbook explains that copyright protects expression, rather than ideas, methods or facts, and that acquisition is automatic without registration formalities. (India; Handbook: Copyright; Work; Registration of Copyright (pp3,9)) 7

Inference/application: Original label artwork, written material and manuals may qualify as expression. This does not confer protection over the underlying medicinal formula or functional process. 2 Original written or artistic descriptions may qualify; the medicine's formula and manufacturing method are not monopolised by copyright. 7

Not established by retrieved sources: Originality, ownership, assignments and any overlap with industrial-design rules require the actual works and agreements. Eligibility and ownership of the actual creative works remain unverified; the historical handbook does not establish current procedural fees or office particulars.

Other IP: packaging design

Established by source: Registered designs concern eligible visual features of an article, such as shape, configuration, pattern or ornament, rather than a principle of construction; the Act requires a new or original design. Section 11 provides 10 years of protection, extendable by 5 years. (India; ss.2(d), 11) 10

Inference/application: A qualifying bottle or packaging appearance may be protectable separately from the medicine; functional formulation or processing know-how is not protected by that appearance right. 10

Not established by retrieved sources: Novelty, prior publication, functionality and the design's eligibility need review of the actual article.

Inventorship, ownership and assignments

Established by source: Subject to s.134, s.6 permits an application by the person claiming to be the true and first inventor, the assignee of that person's right to apply, or the specified legal representative, alone or jointly. Sections 7(2)-(3) require assignment-based proof of the right to apply and naming the inventor; s.10(6) addresses the inventorship declaration. Under s.28(1), mention as inventor does not itself confer or remove patent rights. (India; ss.6, 7(2)-(3), 10(6), 28(1)) 6 Section 68 requires an assignment of a patent or share, mortgage, licence or other patent interest to be in a written, duly executed document embodying the parties' rights and obligations. Section 69(1) requires the person acquiring the specified patent title or interest to apply to register that title or notice of interest; s.69(3) addresses proof of title and disputes. (India; ss.68, 69(1)-(3)) 11

Inference/application: You report “Our employee created the extraction process during paid work, a university laboratory optimized stability under a collaboration agreement, and a freelance designer made our label.” Identify the human contributors to the claimed invention separately from the person or entity entitled to apply. If the company relies on assignment of the right to apply, it needs the applicable proof while the inventor remains identified. Employment, payment and a university collaboration do not supply that proof in this record. The company's claimed title remains unresolved until the contributions and chain of title are checked; mention as inventor does not itself confer patent rights. 6 For a transaction in an existing patent, assess the written, duly executed instrument and registration of the acquired title or interest under these provisions. Keep that separate from proof of an assignment of the right to apply before grant. Inspect the actual employment, university and other agreements for invention scope, retained rights and execution; payment or a confidentiality clause does not establish the required assignment here. These patent provisions do not decide copyright ownership of artwork. 11

Not established by retrieved sources: The actual inventive contributions, employment or research terms, university obligations and chain of title need the relevant records and agreements. These passages do not decide the particular dispute. Whether a signed agreement covers this invention or patent, who could assign it, any retained rights and the registration position remain unverified. Patent rules do not decide copyright ownership of artwork or manuals.

Step-by-step strategy

Inference/application — Preserve confidentiality and decide what to disclose: Limit access to non-public formulae and process parameters, use appropriate confidentiality agreements and document who receives the information. 1 Give the patent drafter the reproducible method, relevant best-method details, biological-material sources and geographical origins. 5
Inference/application — Assess the proposed patent claims: Document the claimed technical contribution and commission a prior-art and patentability assessment before selecting claims. 13 Assess patentability and freedom to operate separately, and coordinate any patent application with the Patent Office route. 4
Inference/application — Verify inventorship and the chain of title: Map each claimed technical contribution to its contributor and inspect employment, university, contractor and assignment documents before naming inventors and applicants. 6 Review the signed chain-of-title documents, invention and patent scope, retained rights and required registration before asserting company ownership or granting a licence. 11
Inference/application — Select the applicable brand and other IP protection: Choose a distinctive brand and conduct clearance before applying for the relevant goods/services. 9 Keep dated artwork/text files and confirm ownership or assignments for commissioned creative material. 2

Facts still needed and conditional outcomes

What are the complete ingredients and quantities, their authoritative-text references, the exact formula, dosage form, route and intended claims? Studying classical texts alone does not supply those details. Inference/application: The classical ASU route first requires medicinal intended use for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder. A formula match alone does not establish that use. Classical status remains unresolved: compare the complete formula and manufacture with a First-Schedule formula. Developing a combination yourself or studying classical texts does not establish either a match or its absence. (s.3(a)) 15 First establish that the product is an ASU medicine on its actual intended use; an ingredient-book match alone does not classify a nonmedicinal product as a medicine. The proprietary category is then conditional on every ingredient meeting the First-Schedule book test, the formulation itself being absent from those formulae, and a non-parenteral route. Calling the product new or proprietary does not verify those facts or establish patentability. (s.3(h)(i)) 8
What evidence verifies the stated ownership/control and establishes the actual applicant's statutory category? Inference/application: You supplied these applicant/entity assertions: “All herbs are cultivated in India and bought from traders; our company has a German majority shareholder.” Verify the actual applicant's incorporation and control, and citizenship/residence where applicable, against section 3(2). Stated Indian ownership or a foreign shareholder alone does not settle that statutory category. Apply prior NBA approval only to the covered applicant and access purpose; company share ownership does not determine ownership of IP. (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) 6 If the applicant falls within section 3(2), assess prior NBA approval for covered access; an Indian manufacturing address does not settle citizenship, residence or foreign control (ss.3(1)-(2); amendment s.5; Biological Diversity Rules, 2024 r.13) 6 For a person outside section 3(2), assess section 7 prior SBB intimation and its actual exemptions for covered commercial access (s.7(1) proviso, s.7(2)-(3); Amendment Act s.9, p.4) 1 The same applicant distinction changes the IP milestone: NBA approval before grant for section 3(2) persons, versus pre-grant registration and applicable commercialisation approval for section 7 persons (s.6(1), s.6(1A), s.6(1B); Amendment Act s.8, pp.3-4) 9

Classical or proprietary medicine

Established by source: Section 3(a) covers ASU medicines intended for internal or external use in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder in humans or animals, and manufactured exclusively according to formulae in the authoritative books listed in the First Schedule. (India; s.3(a)) 15 An ASU patent or proprietary medicine must contain only ingredients mentioned in formulae in First-Schedule authoritative books; the formulation itself must not be included there, and parenteral medicines are excluded. (India; s.3(h)(i)) 8

Inference/application: The classical ASU route first requires medicinal intended use for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease or disorder. A formula match alone does not establish that use. Classical status remains unresolved: compare the complete formula and manufacture with a First-Schedule formula. Developing a combination yourself or studying classical texts does not establish either a match or its absence. 15 First establish that the product is an ASU medicine on its actual intended use; an ingredient-book match alone does not classify a nonmedicinal product as a medicine. The proprietary category is then conditional on every ingredient meeting the First-Schedule book test, the formulation itself being absent from those formulae, and a non-parenteral route. Calling the product new or proprietary does not verify those facts or establish patentability. 8

Established by source: Section 3 requires prior NBA approval for the specified access purposes by persons within s.3(2), which distinguishes non-citizens, the specified non-resident citizens and covered foreign/foreign-controlled entities.
